name: The Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep)
scope: A crescent-shaped gash in the western Pacific seafloor near Guam, holding the deepest point on Earth. T1: the Challenger Deep is so deep (~10,935 m, almost 11 km down) that if you dropped Mount Everest in, its peak would still be over 2 km underwater -- the deepest place on the planet. T2 (invert): the trench was first sounded and named by the 1875 voyage of a British ship -- HMS Challenger -- which is where 'Challenger Deep' (and later the space shuttle) got its name. T3: in 1960 two men, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, rode a bathyscaphe called the Trieste to the bottom -- a 5-hour descent, a window cracking on the way down -- the first (and for 52 years the only) humans to reach it. T4: at the bottom the pressure is over 1,000 times sea-level pressure (~1,086 bar), like the weight of an elephant balanced on your thumbnail. T5: the trench is not a crack but a SUBDUCTION zone -- the old, cold Pacific Plate bends and dives beneath the Mariana Plate, and the deep is the crease where crust plunges back into the mantle (teach: subduction). Extra rungs: in 2012 filmmaker James Cameron dived it SOLO in the Deepsea Challenger, the deepest solo dive ever; even in total darkness at the bottom, no sunlight ever reaches it, so life there survives on 'marine snow' drifting down from far above; serpentine mud volcanoes vent along the subducting slab; it is a protected US marine national monument.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Britannica 'Challenger Deep'; Wikipedia 'Challenger Deep' and 'Mariana Trench'; deepseachallenge.com (Cameron 2012 solo dive); revised-depth study (ScienceDirect, Challenger Deep transects). Grokipedia checked first (page blocked to direct fetch; corroborated via the above).
framing_note: Scene-led ocean-superlative voice: lead with the number/darkness as the hook, make the KNOWABLE thing the answer -- never 'What is the deepest point?'. Accuracy rail: keep the ~10,935 m depth and the 1960 Trieste / 2012 Cameron attributions exact and distinct (Trieste = two men Piccard+Walsh, first ever; Deepsea Challenger = Cameron, solo). Dinner-test payoff = the 1960 Trieste descent (two men in a steel ball at the bottom of the world). Distractors stay live with other real deeps (Tonga/Kermadec/Puerto Rico trenches, other superlatives). LANE: the deepest-fish (snailfish) belongs to the ANIMAL bank -- if a bottom-life rung appears, keep the answer the PLACE-fact (no sunlight, marine-snow food web), not a creature's anatomy.

name: The Great Barrier Reef
scope: The world's largest coral reef system, off the Queensland coast of Australia. T1: stretching over 2,300 km, it is the only living thing on Earth big enough to see from space -- the largest living structure on the planet. T2 (invert): this colossus is built entirely by billions of tiny soft-bodied animals -- coral POLYPS, each smaller than a fingernail -- laying down limestone skeletons over thousands of years. T3: it is not one reef but a system of about 2,900 separate reefs and 900 islands scattered across the Coral Sea. T4: once a year, a few nights after the November full moon, the WHOLE reef spawns at the same instant -- billions of polyps release pink-and-orange egg bundles in a synchronized underwater 'snowstorm' (mass coral spawning). T5: corals get their color and much of their food from tiny algae (zooxanthellae) living inside them; when the water gets too warm the coral expels the algae and turns bone-white -- coral BLEACHING (teach the term as an ocean-warming process). Extra rungs: today's living reef grew over just the last ~6,000-8,000 years, on the drowned foundation of far older reefs, as seas rose after the last Ice Age; the naturally heart-shaped Heart Reef; it is a UNESCO World Heritage site the size of Italy.
source: WebSearch corroboration: ESA 'Earth from Space: World's largest living structure'; NOAA oceanservice.noaa.gov 'largest structure'; Wikipedia 'Great Barrier Reef'; Great Barrier Reef Foundation 'coral spawning' explainer; Reef Authority (GBRMPA) 'coral spawning 101'.
framing_note: Wonder voice: the reef's SIZE and the spawning event are the hooks; keep answers to named, retellable facts (the polyp builders, the once-a-year spawn, bleaching). Accuracy rail: 'visible from space / largest living structure' is correct; the builders are animal polyps, but the reef itself is a PLACE/structure -- keep answers about the reef, its formation, and reef-scale processes. Dinner-test payoff = the synchronized mass coral spawning after the full moon. LANE: sea turtles, dugongs, and reef fish are ANIMAL-bank subjects -- do not build a creature-biology rung; the polyp appears only as the reef's builder, not as an anatomy lesson.

name: The Pacific Ocean & Point Nemo
scope: Earth's largest and deepest ocean. T1 (invert): one ocean is so vast it is bigger than every continent and island on Earth put together -- covering about a third of the whole planet's surface: the Pacific. T2: it got its calm-sounding name from Ferdinand Magellan in 1520, who called it 'Mar Pacifico' ('peaceful sea') after finally reaching still water beyond the storms of South America. T3: the single spot farthest from any land is Point Nemo (48deg53'S 123deg24'W) -- so remote that when the Space Station passes overhead, the nearest humans are the astronauts in orbit, not anyone on a ship. T4: right near Point Nemo is the 'spacecraft cemetery,' the patch of empty ocean where space agencies deliberately crash old satellites and space stations because it is the farthest place on Earth from people. T5: the Pacific is ringed by the 'Ring of Fire' -- a horseshoe of volcanoes and earthquakes, home to roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes, where its plates dive beneath the surrounding continents (teach: the Ring of Fire). Extra rungs: you could sail a straight line ~20,000 miles across it without touching land; it holds the deepest point on Earth (the Challenger Deep -- cross-ref) and more islands than the rest of the oceans combined; it is slowly SHRINKING a few cm a year as the Atlantic widens.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Wikipedia 'Pacific Ocean' and 'Pole of inaccessibility'; NOAA Ocean Exploration 'How big is the Pacific Ocean?'; Britannica 'oceanic pole of inaccessibility (Point Nemo)'.
framing_note: Ocean-superlative voice: put the big number/superlative in the stem and make the named thing the answer (bigger-than-all-land -> the Pacific; farthest-from-land -> Point Nemo). Accuracy rail: the Magellan naming is a one-line attribution-of-a-name-to-a-place (keep it a naming fact, not a full voyage-history rung); Point Nemo coordinates and the ISS-is-nearest fact are exact. Dinner-test payoff = Point Nemo (the loneliest place on Earth, where astronauts overhead are the closest people). Distractors: other real oceans/seas and other 'poles of inaccessibility' keep the four choices live.

name: The Bay of Fundy (highest tides on Earth)
scope: A funnel-shaped bay between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, Canada. T1 (invert): twice a day so much seawater pours in that the tide rises as high as a four-story building -- about 16.3 m at Burntcoat Head, the highest tides recorded anywhere on Earth. T2: each tide moves roughly 160 billion tonnes of water in or out -- more than the combined flow of every river on Earth -- squeezed through the narrow Minas Passage. T3: the tides climb so high because of RESONANCE -- the bay is shaped so the time for water to slosh from mouth to head and back (~13 hours) nearly matches the ~12.5-hour rhythm of the ocean tide, so each incoming pulse piles onto the last (teach: tidal resonance). T4: at Hopewell Rocks the falling tide bares towering 'flowerpot' rock pillars with trees growing on top -- you can walk the sea floor at low tide and paddle a kayak over the very same spot hours later. T5: at Saint John the rising tide is so powerful it reverses a river and its rapids -- the famous 'Reversing Falls,' where the water briefly runs uphill. Extra rungs: a tidal BORE (a standing wave) travels upriver against the current as the tide turns; the highest surge ever recorded (~21.6 m) came in the 1869 Saxby Gale.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Wikipedia 'Burntcoat, Nova Scotia' (16.3 m, Guinness 1975); surfertoday.com 'Bay of Fundy world's largest tidal range'; fundydiscovery.ca 'Fundy Fun Facts' (160 billion tonnes / resonance).
framing_note: Scene-led: the 16 m rise and the 160-billion-tonne flow are the hooks; the answer is the named place / named feature, never 'What is the highest tide?'. Accuracy rail: keep 16.3 m (Burntcoat Head) and the ~160 billion tonnes/tide figures exact, and explain the RESONANCE mechanism correctly (matched sloshing period, not just the funnel shape alone). Dinner-test payoff = 160 billion tonnes per tide, more than all the world's rivers combined. LANE: whales feeding in Fundy are an ANIMAL-bank aside -- keep every answer the PLACE and its tides.

name: The Sargasso Sea (a sea with no shores)
scope: A vast, calm region of the North Atlantic with no coastline. T1 (invert): in the middle of the Atlantic sits a 'sea' with no shore on any side -- bounded not by land but by circling currents: the Sargasso Sea. T2: its four 'walls' are four great ocean currents that swirl in a slow loop called the North Atlantic Gyre, and everything that floats gets trapped in the calm center. T3: it is named for the golden floating seaweed -- SARGASSUM -- that carpets its surface in drifting rafts; unlike ordinary seaweed it never attaches to the bottom, living its whole life adrift. T4: this is the one place on Earth where European and American eels are born -- every eel in every European and eastern-American river hatched HERE, then swam thousands of km to a river and, years later, all the way back to the Sargasso to spawn and die. T5: its dead-calm stillness terrified sailors -- becalmed ships could sit windless for weeks in the center; it overlaps the legendary 'Bermuda Triangle,' and Columbus logged its weed rafts in 1492. Extra rung: its water is warm, deep-blue, and clear because it is nutrient-poor, ringed by Bermuda.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Wikipedia 'Sargasso Sea'; Forbes 'Scientists Show Eel Breeding Grounds For The First Time' (2022); ScienceAlert 'Scientists Track Eels to Their Ocean Breeding Grounds'.
framing_note: Wonder-riddle voice: the 'sea with no coast' paradox is the hook; the answer is the named sea / the current-boundary / the eel birthplace. Accuracy rail: the eel-spawning fact is a PLACE-fact (the Sargasso is where they are born) -- the exact spawning has been inferred/newly tracked, so keep it 'the eels' breeding ground', not a claim we have filmed the eggs. Dinner-test payoff = every European eel was born in this one shore-less sea and swims back across an ocean to die there. LANE: the eel's life cycle/biology belongs to the ANIMAL bank -- keep the answer the sea's role as birthplace, not eel physiology.

name: The Red Sea (a new ocean being born)
scope: The warm sea splitting Africa from Arabia -- a young ocean basin in the making. T1: the Red Sea is not a fixed sea -- it is getting WIDER every year, because Africa and Arabia are slowly tearing apart (about 1-2 cm a year, roughly as fast as your fingernails grow). T2 (invert): geologists call it a baby ocean -- a brand-new ocean basin being born; in tens of millions of years it could grow as wide as today's Atlantic (teach: sea-floor spreading / a spreading rift). T3: it is one arm of a giant crack in the Earth that meets the East African Rift and the Gulf of Aden at the AFAR TRIPLE JUNCTION, where three tectonic plates pull away from one another at once. T4: on its floor lie deadly 'brine pools' -- lakes of water so hot and so salty (denser than the sea itself) that they pool at the bottom like underwater ponds, with their own shorelines and lapping shores. T5: despite being one of the warmest and saltiest seas, its coral reefs are among the most heat-TOLERANT on Earth, thriving in water that would bleach and kill reefs elsewhere. Extra rung: it may be named 'Red' for seasonal blooms of reddish Trichodesmium algae (label as one leading hypothesis, not certain); it is extra-salty because strong sun evaporates it and almost no rivers refill it.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Grokipedia 'Red Sea Rift' (surfaced first); Wikipedia 'Red Sea Rift' and 'Red Sea'; Eos 'Are We Seeing a New Ocean Starting to Form in Africa?'.
framing_note: Earth-process wonder: the widening / new-ocean idea is the payoff, taught concretely (plates pulling apart at a known rate). Accuracy rail: spreading rate ~1-2 cm/yr and the Afar triple junction are exact; label the 'why it is called Red' as a hypothesis, not settled fact. Dinner-test payoff = 'a new ocean is being born here' (the sea itself is a growing ocean basin). LANE / history_overlap: the biblical 'parting of the Red Sea' is HISTORY/THEOLOGY-bank territory -- keep it out of this earth-science ladder (at most one non-load-bearing mention). Reef corals appear as a place/heat-tolerance fact, not coral biology.
history_overlap: History/theology bank owns the biblical 'parting of the Red Sea' episode -- keep it OUT of this earth-science ladder (at most a single non-load-bearing mention).

name: The Great Blue Hole (Belize)
scope: A giant marine sinkhole in the Lighthouse Reef atoll off Belize. T1 (invert): from above, the turquoise Caribbean has a perfect dark-blue circle punched into it -- a sinkhole about 318 m wide and 124 m deep: the Great Blue Hole. T2: it was not always underwater -- during the Ice Age, when seas were far lower, this was a DRY limestone cave on land; when the ice melted and the ocean rose, the cave roof collapsed and seawater flooded in. T3: divers deep inside find giant STALACTITES hanging from the overhangs -- and stalactites can only grow in air-filled caves, hard proof the place was once bone-dry (teach: stalactites as a clue to a drowned cave). T4: around 90 m down, divers hit a layer of poisonous hydrogen-sulfide with no oxygen and no light -- everything below it is lifeless, dark, and still. T5: it sits inside the Belize Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef in the Northern Hemisphere and second in the world only to Australia's, which Charles Darwin praised as the finest reef in the West Indies (1842). Extra rung: Jacques Cousteau explored and mapped it in 1971 and made it world-famous, ranking it among his top-five dive sites on Earth.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Wikipedia 'Great Blue Hole' (318 m x 124 m; H2S ~90 m; stalactite dating); geologyscience.com 'Great Blue Hole'; Forbes 'How Jacques Cousteau's 1971 expedition' (Cousteau fame).
framing_note: Scene-led: the perfect blue circle is the hook; the answer is the drowned-cave origin or the stalactite clue, never 'What is a sinkhole?'. Accuracy rail: keep 318 m/124 m and the Ice-Age drowned-cave sequence exact -- the stalactites are the LOAD-BEARING evidence it was once dry. Dinner-test payoff = it was a dry cave you could have walked into during the Ice Age, then the roof fell and the sea poured in. LANE: sharks that cruise the hole are ANIMAL-bank -- keep the answer the geology (karst collapse, stalactites, the H2S layer).

name: The Yucatan cenotes & the dinosaur crater
scope: The flooded sinkholes of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula and the buried crater they trace. T1: across the flat Yucatan jungle there are almost NO surface rivers -- instead, rainwater collects underground and opens the roof in thousands of round, clear-blue sinkholes called CENOTES (teach: cenote = a collapsed limestone sinkhole; from the Maya ts'onot, 'sacred well'). T2 (invert): the densest cenotes trace a giant, near-perfect ARC across the peninsula -- a 'Ring of Cenotes' -- because they sit right above the buried rim of the crater left by the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs 66 million years ago (the Chicxulub impact). T3: that impactor was about 10 km across and blasted a crater roughly 180 km wide; the shattered rim rock drains water differently, which is why the sinkholes line up above it. T4: beneath the jungle the flooded cenotes link into the LONGEST underwater cave systems on Earth -- Sistema Sac Actun maps hundreds of km of submerged passages (with an even longer system, Ox Bel Ha, recently reported nearby). T5: to the ancient Maya, cenotes were sacred gateways to the underworld; at Chichen Itza the 'Sacred Cenote' was dredged to reveal offerings of gold, jade, and human sacrifices (present as archaeology). Extra rungs: cenotes form by KARST dissolution (rainwater slowly eating limestone); divers have found some of the oldest human skeletons in the Americas (e.g. 'Naia,' ~13,000 years old) in these flooded caves; the coast meets the Mesoamerican Reef.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Northwestern Univ. Karst Geochemistry (Monroy-Rios) 'Chicxulub and Ring of Cenotes'; UNESCO tentative list 'Ring of cenotes of Chicxulub Crater'; Wikipedia 'Cenote'; CINDAQ (Sac Actun / Ox Bel Ha survey lengths).
framing_note: Earth-science wonder braided with archaeology: the crater-ring reveal is the payoff, taught concretely (why sinkholes line up over a buried crater rim). Accuracy rail: the Chicxulub impact (66 Mya, ~10 km impactor, ~180 km crater) and the cenote-ring alignment are well established; keep the underwater-cave length claim conservative ('among the world's longest', Sac Actun ~370+ km) and let the build verify the current record. Dinner-test payoff = the Ring of Cenotes is the surface fingerprint of the dinosaur-killer crater. VISION: the Maya sacred-cenote/human-sacrifice rung is indigenous-civilization content -- present it factually and respectfully (documented archaeology), neither romanticized nor sensationalized, no moral verdict. LANE/overlap: keep every answer the PLACE (karst, crater ring, sacred well), not a Maya political timeline (history bank).
history_overlap: History bank may cover the Maya civilization and Chichen Itza as a human-history episode; keep this ladder's answers on the PLACE's geology (cenote karst, the crater's surface ring, the flooded caves) and the cenotes' sacred-well USE, not a Maya political/dynastic timeline.

name: Monterey Bay kelp forests
scope: The towering underwater forests of California's Monterey Bay. T1 (invert): along the California coast grow underwater 'forests' as tall as a 15-story building -- made not of trees but of giant KELP, a golden seaweed anchored to the sea floor. T2: giant kelp is the fastest-growing life in the sea -- up to about 60 cm (2 feet) in a single day, racing a whole blade toward the sunlight at the surface. T3: it has no true roots -- it grips bare rock with a claw-like HOLDFAST, and each frond is floated upward by its own gas-filled bladder called a PNEUMATOCYST (teach both terms). T4: the kelp forest is a whole vertical habitat -- a floating canopy on top, an understory below, a shaded floor beneath -- and it stays standing only because sea otters eat the urchins that would otherwise mow it down (a keystone-balance PLACE-fact). T5: kelp forests grow only in cold, nutrient-rich water, which is why they ring the cool coasts of the world (California, Chile, South Africa's Great African Sea Forest, Tasmania) but never the warm tropics. Extra rung: giant kelp is an ALGA, not a plant -- no flowers, no true roots, no seeds.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Monterey Bay Aquarium 'Giant kelp'; Guinness World Records 'Fastest-growing marine plant'; Wikipedia 'Macrocystis'.
framing_note: Wonder voice: the forest-under-the-sea image and the 60-cm-a-day growth are the hooks; keep answers the named place / named part (holdfast, pneumatocyst) / the growth superlative. Accuracy rail: ~60 cm/day is the record growth figure; kelp is an alga (not a plant) -- teach that. Dinner-test payoff = the fastest-growing living thing in the sea, ~2 feet a DAY. LANE: the otter-and-urchin balance appears only as the reason the FOREST stands (a place/ecosystem fact) -- do not turn it into sea-otter anatomy/behavior, which is ANIMAL-bank.

name: The Sundarbans (mangrove coast)
scope: The world's largest mangrove forest, where the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta meets the Bay of Bengal. T1 (invert): where two of Asia's greatest rivers empty into the sea lies the largest mangrove forest on Earth -- the Sundarbans, a maze of tidal islands where trees grow with their roots standing in salt water. T2: mangroves are among the very few trees that can live in the sea -- their tangled stilt-roots poke up out of the mud to BREATHE, and their leaves sweat out the salt the roots cannot block (teach: mangrove / breathing roots as a coastal landscape). T3: that wall of roots is a natural sea-wall -- mangrove coasts blunt storm surges and cyclones, and in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, villages sheltered behind mangroves suffered far less damage than bare coasts. T4: the waterlogged root-mud is a carbon TRAP -- mangroves lock away 'blue carbon' many times faster than an ordinary forest, burying it in the airless mud for centuries. T5: the Sundarbans is the last place on Earth where tigers swim between islands and patrol a mangrove coast -- the only tiger population that lives in a mangrove (a PLACE-fact). Extra rung: the tangled roots are a nursery where countless fish and shrimp begin life; the forest is split ~60% India, ~40% Bangladesh.
source: WebSearch corroboration: MDPI Forests 'cyclone vulnerability in the world's largest mangrove forest, the Sundarbans'; Science / PNAS studies on mangrove buffering in the 2004 tsunami and Indian super-cyclone; Wikipedia 'Sundarbans'.
framing_note: Coastal-landscape wonder: the storm-buffer payoff is taught concretely (roots blunt the surge; 2004 tsunami evidence). Accuracy rail: the largest-mangrove-forest and 2004-tsunami-buffering facts are established; keep the tiger rung a PLACE-fact (only mangrove with a tiger population), not tiger biology. Dinner-test payoff = the mangrove wall that saved villages from the 2004 tsunami. LANE: the Bengal tiger's biology/behavior is ANIMAL-bank -- the tiger appears only as a signature of THIS place; the trees' salt-filtering is treated as landscape/earth-process, not botany-for-its-own-sake.

name: The Norwegian maelstroms (Saltstraumen & Moskstraumen)
scope: The tidal whirlpools of the Norwegian coast -- the same wonder in two named places. T1 (invert): four times a day, near the town of Bodo, the tide forces a whole fjord's worth of water through a strait only ~150 m wide, creating the strongest tidal current ever measured -- up to ~40 km/h (22 knots): SALTSTRAUMEN. T2: the rushing water spins into whirlpools -- MAELSTROMS -- up to 10 m across and several meters deep, powerful enough to swallow a small boat. T3: it happens because about 400 million cubic meters of seawater try to squeeze through that narrow gap every six hours as the tide turns -- a narrow throat makes a furious current (teach: why a constriction speeds a tidal flow). T4: farther south, off the Lofoten Islands, the MOSKSTRAUMEN is the maelstrom of legend -- for centuries it terrified sailors and inspired Edgar Allan Poe's tale 'A Descent into the Maelstrom' and Jules Verne. Extra rung: the word 'maelstrom' itself comes from an old Dutch/Norse phrase meaning 'grinding stream'.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Grokipedia 'Saltstraumen' (surfaced first); Wikipedia 'Saltstraumen' (40 km/h, 400 million m3 / 6 h, 150 m strait, 10 m whirlpools); VisitNorway 'Saltstraumen'; Wikipedia 'Moskstraumen' / Poe 'A Descent into the Maelstrom'.
framing_note: A tightly coherent two-place ladder on ONE wonder (Norwegian tidal maelstroms); every rung names its specific place so the place-anchor holds. Accuracy rail (LOAD-BEARING): the STRONGEST-measured current is Saltstraumen (near Bodo); the LITERARY maelstrom that inspired Poe and Verne is the MOSKSTRAUMEN off Lofoten -- do NOT credit Poe to Saltstraumen. Scene-led: the 40 km/h / whirlpool-swallows-a-boat image is the hook. Dinner-test payoff = the 10 m whirlpools of Saltstraumen, the strongest tidal current on Earth. Distractors: other real whirlpools (Corryvreckan, Old Sow, Naruto) keep the choices live.

name: The Maldives & coral atolls (Darwin's theory)
scope: A nation of ring-shaped coral reefs in the Indian Ocean, and the puzzle of how atolls form. T1 (invert): the Maldives is a country of ~1,200 islands, but almost none rises more than ~1.5 m above the sea -- the lowest, flattest nation on Earth, built entirely of ring-shaped coral reefs called ATOLLS (teach: atoll = a ring of reef around a central lagoon; the word itself comes from the Maldivian Dhivehi 'atholhu'). T2: Charles Darwin solved the riddle of how a ring of coral ends up in open ocean with no island in the middle -- a volcano once stood there, the volcano slowly SANK, and the coral kept growing upward toward the light, leaving a ring where the island used to be (Darwin's subsidence theory, 1842). T3: for a century it was only a theory -- until, in the 1950s, scientists drilled straight down through Bikini and Enewetok atolls and struck solid VOLCANIC rock deep beneath the coral, exactly as Darwin had predicted. T4: because an atoll is ALIVE, it can grow upward as the sea rises -- but only so fast; the Maldives now sits on the front line of sea-level rise and has even discussed buying higher land abroad for its people. Extra rung: the whole nation has no bedrock at all -- every island is made of coral sand and reef rock; the calm central lagoon is shallow and turquoise.
source: WebSearch corroboration: Britannica 'Darwinian subsidence theory'; Wikipedia 'The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs' (Darwin 1842); MIT Oceans 'Coral Reefs and Sinking Islands'; Eos 'Rethinking Darwin's Theory of Atoll Formation'.
framing_note: Earth-science wonder: Darwin's sinking-volcano idea is the payoff, taught as a three-step picture (fringing reef -> sinking island + lagoon -> ring), then confirmed by the atoll drilling. Accuracy rail: attribute the subsidence theory to Darwin (1842) and the confirming cores to the 1950s Bikini/Enewetok drilling; keep the Maldives-is-lowest-country fact exact (~1.5 m average). Dinner-test payoff = a coral ring marks the grave of a drowned volcano. LANE/overlap: Bikini and Enewetok are also famous for 1940s-50s NUCLEAR TESTS -- that is HISTORY-bank territory; keep the Bikini rung on the scientific DRILLING that confirmed Darwin, not the bomb tests.
history_overlap: Bikini/Enewetok atolls are also famous for 1940s-50s US nuclear tests -- that belongs to the history bank; keep the Bikini rung strictly on the 1950s scientific drilling that confirmed Darwin's subsidence theory.
